name: Pashupatinath Temple
label: Pashupatinath
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Arya Ghat' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Arya Ghat' (way/80913711): middle (88 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q380384: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Major Hindu temple complex on the Bagmati River.

text.description:
Pashupatinath is a Hindu temple to Pashupati, a form of Shiva, set on the banks of the Bagmati River. It is one of the oldest and most important religious complexes in South Asia, and part of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage listing since 1979. The main temple is a Newari-style pagoda with copper roofs covered in gold and a gold pinnacle, about 23 metres tall. It stands among hundreds of smaller shrines (518 mini-temples) across a precinct of 246 hectares. The temple is recorded as early as 400 CE, and its present form dates from a renovation in 1692.

The view works because one frame can hold the golden roofs, the river and the stone ghats (the bathing and ritual steps along the water). From the stone steps on the eastern bank facing the aarati platform (often called Arya Ghat), you can frame the temple's roofs together with the river, the ghats and the evening ceremony. Guides treat the eastern bank as the best all-round angle. The hilltop Pashupatinath Viewpoint is a good alternative if you want a slightly higher, wider look over the complex, its roofs, the river and the valley.

This is a living place of worship, so photograph with care. Keep your distance from mourners and from any cremation, never use flash near the rites, and leave drones at home.
text.geographic_location: Pashupatinath stands on the banks of the sacred Bagmati River in Kathmandu. Steps on the eastern bank face the aarati platform.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; navigate to the Pashupatinath temple area on the Bagmati River by map. The temple is about 44 metres to the north-east of that point. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the roofs, river and ghats into one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the golden roofs. The ultra-wide (0.5x) suits the steps and the crowd in the foreground, but the temple will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Arya Ghat (east bank of the Bagmati, on the stone steps facing the aarati platform). The temple's golden pagoda roofs across the river, with the ghats and the evening aarati in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the roofs on an upper third, with the river and ghats filling the lower part. Keep the steps or the water's edge in the foreground to give a sense of depth. For a wider, higher view of the whole complex, try the Pashupatinath Viewpoint on the hill as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gold roof to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out. For the evening ceremony, hold the phone steady against your body or a rail and let night mode work if the app offers it. A Live Photo can catch the movement of the ceremony. Do not use flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, roughly 3:30 to 5:00 PM, when the light falls on the golden roof. Stay on for the evening aarati.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship and a World Heritage precinct: photography is not allowed inside the main sanctum and non-Hindus cannot enter it, so check the official site before you go for current visiting and ticket rules.

name: Swayambhunath
label: Swayambhunath
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Swayambhunath Stupa' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q12946982: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Hilltop stupa with watching Buddha eyes and views over the valley.

text.description: Swayambhunath sits on top of a hill west of Kathmandu city, and it is an ancient Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage site in the Kathmandu Valley. The white dome carries a cube painted with the Eyes of Buddha, which look out in all four directions. Above the cube are thirteen gold-plated rings that stand for the stages before nirvana. The hill is also home to families of monkeys, which is why many people call it the Monkey Temple. It photographs well because the eyes, the gold spire, the prayer flags and the valley below all fit into one climb. The stupa was renovated in May 2010, its first major renovation since 1921, and re-gilded with 20 kg of gold. It was damaged in the April 2015 earthquake, so some areas may be closed. UNESCO listed the site in 1979. Pratap Malla built the long eastern stairway in the seventeenth century, and a long staircase from the east leads directly to the main platform. The most popular shot is from the upper terrace on the northeast/east side of the dome, looking back across the valley. The gilded spire and Buddha eyes fill the foreground and the valley opens out below. For a second angle, try the World Peace Pond, where the gilded statue stands in the pool with the climb behind it. Maha Manjushree Temple gives a wider view of the whole hilltop. Go early if you can, as morning light falls on the eastern face and haze builds later.
text.geographic_location: Swayambhunath stands on a hill in the Kathmandu Valley, west of Kathmandu city. The stupa is on the hilltop and the city and valley spread out below it.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near here; the site lies west of central Kathmandu. The long staircase from the east leads straight up to the main platform. A road also runs around the hill from the south to the south-west entrance. From the phone icon on the map the subject is right beside you, so there is no extra walk once you are on the terrace. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the dome and spire with some of the valley behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole terrace, flags and view together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Buddha eyes and the gold rings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look back toward the valley, with the gilded spire and Buddha eyes in the foreground and the Kathmandu Valley spread out below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the Buddha eyes on an upper line, with the valley filling the lower part of the frame. Keep the spire upright by lining it up with a vertical gridline. For a wider, calmer view of the whole hilltop complex, try Maha Manjushree Temple as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Buddha eyes to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold and white do not burn out against the sky. Take a few frames, as flags and visitors keep moving. Check for no-photography signs before shooting inside any shrine, and ask before photographing worshippers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before haze builds up, when the sun lights the eastern face. Clear views of the Himalaya are seasonal, mainly October to February.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship and a World Heritage Site where an entrance fee may apply and some areas may be closed after earthquake damage, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Monkeys on the site can be bold around phones and food, so keep a firm grip on your phone.
From the upper terrace the valley is seen looking back from the dome, with the gilded spire and Buddha eyes in the foreground (from the viewpoint advice, not the main text).

name: Garden of Dreams
label: Garden of Dreams
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Garden of Dreams' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/85650618: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Garden of Dreams' (147 m across).

text.description:
The Garden of Dreams is a calm, walled garden tucked into the busy streets near Thamel. It was laid out in 1920 as a private garden for Field Marshal Kaiser Sumsher Rana and designed by Kishore Narshingh. The look is Edwardian in spirit: neat, straight lines of pavilions, pergolas, urns and balustrades set against softer, more natural planting. Around 6,895 square metres of garden remain, with three pavilions, an amphitheatre and several ponds. After decades of neglect it was restored between 2000 and 2007, and it is now open to visitors.

It photographs well because everything is arranged around the paths and water, so the garden gives you ready-made frames. The classic shot is from the central lotus pond, looking back toward the pavilions, with the buildings and flower beds reflected in the water. Use the paths as leading lines and let the pavilions sit in the upper half of the picture, with their reflection below.

Two other good frames are inside the garden. At Barkha Pavilion, let the architecture fill the background and put a person in the foreground. At the Open Air Theatre, frame the curved seating against the greenery. Keep your phone steady on a railing or low wall rather than relying on a tripod. Check the official site before you go, as some rules and closed areas may apply.
text.geographic_location: The Garden of Dreams is in Kaiser Mahal, on Tridevi Sadak in central Kathmandu. It lies across the street from the former Royal Palace, at the entrance to the Thamel tourist area and near Kantipath.
text.directions_text: No nearby stops are listed for this spot, so start from Thamel, which is right next to the garden, and head toward the former Royal Palace side of the area. The garden is in Kaiser Mahal on Tridevi Sadak, near Thamel and Kantipath, so you can navigate to it by name: the Garden of Dreams (Kaiser Mahal). Once inside, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the garden at the central pond. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pond view, which covers the pavilions and their reflection in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavilions are cut off, and use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out details such as an urn or pergola.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look back toward the pavilions, with the pond, the surrounding pavilions and the flower beds reflected in the water, framed by the pathways. For a different view, try Barkha Pavilion or the Open Air Theatre.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on the lower third line, so the pavilions and their reflection balance. Let the pathways lead the eye into the picture. For an alternative, fill the frame with Barkha Pavilion and put a person in front of it, or frame the curved Open Air Theatre against the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pavilions to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone as still as you can for sharp reflections, and keep the lens clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the water is still enough to reflect the pavilions.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed garden, so check the official site before you go for current entry rules, restrictions on photography equipment and any closed areas.

name: Thamel
label: Thamel
notes: Busy tourist quarter with colourful shops and signs.

text.description: Thamel is Kathmandu's best-known tourist neighbourhood, a tangle of narrow alleys packed with shops, cafés, restaurants, guest houses and trekking-gear stalls. The name comes from Tha Bahi, a Newar name, and the area has been the centre of the visitor trade for over four decades, since the hippie days when artists came to Nepal and stayed for weeks. It photographs well because everything is close together and busy: shopfronts spill goods onto the street, signs stack above each other, and cars, cycle rickshaws, two-wheelers and hundreds of people share the same narrow lanes. Typical things to look for are handicrafts, woollen items, souvenirs and trekking gear laid out at the front of shops, which make good close-up details. For a phone, the best pictures are usually of the street life rather than one building. Walk slowly, look for a lane with a clear line of sight, and wait a few seconds for a gap in the traffic or a passer-by to walk into your frame. Keep an eye on your surroundings, because vehicles squeeze past pedestrians here. Ask before taking close portraits of shopkeepers or vendors. The phone icon on the map is a short walk east of the middle of Thamel, so you can reach it first and then walk west into the lanes with your phone ready.
text.geographic_location: Thamel is a commercial neighbourhood in central Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal. It lies about 1.4 km north of Kathmandu's Durbar Square, close to Kwabahal, JP Road, Paknajol and the Sanchaya Kosh road.
text.directions_text: There is no station or stop at this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the Thamel area; from Durbar Square it is about 1.4 km to the north. From there Thamel is about 6 minutes on foot to the west. Keep walking west into the lanes. The phone icon on the map is about 390 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for street scenes. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the tightest alleys when you want to fit in the shopfronts and signs above. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as goods on display, without stepping into people's way.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 390 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Then walk west into the lanes and stop at a corner or a wider junction, where you can shoot down a street without blocking it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use a lane as a leading line, with the shopfronts on both sides and a person or rickshaw as a point of interest. Keep your phone level so the narrow buildings do not lean. For detail shots, fill the frame with a single stall or sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on your main subject, such as a face, a sign or a rickshaw, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright signs are not washed out. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a wall or post. Live Photos can capture the movement of passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer for clear shots of the lanes. In the evening, signs and shop lights come on and give the street more colour, but it will be busier.

text.access_note: Thamel is a district of open public streets with private shops and businesses, so be polite when photographing people and inside premises; check the official site before you go if you plan to enter any specific venue.

name: Indra Chowk
label: Indra Chowk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Akash Bhairav Temple' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Akash Bhairab Temple' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7371674706: the OpenStreetMap point 'Indra Chowk'.
notes: Old market square with the Akash Bhairav shrine.

text.description: Indra Chowk is one of the old ceremonial and market squares on the historic trade street running through Kathmandu. Several streets meet here, and it is busy with shoppers, pilgrims and stalls selling beads and cloth. The large Akash Bhairav temple on the western side is the symbol of the square. Its ground floor holds shops, and a flight of stairs leads up to the big mask of Akash Bhairav, the 'god of the sky'. That makes it a good photo spot: old merchant houses, a lit shrine and street life all fit into one frame. On the eastern side, Raki Bazaar is a twisting alley of small bead shops. Wide Shukra Path runs south towards New Road, lined with white-washed houses built after the 1934 earthquake. The square also hosts festival processions. During Indra Jatra the chariots of Kumari, Ganesh and Bhairav are pulled through it. For your phone, the best view is from the Akash Bhairav Temple side, looking across the junction, with the shrine window and lamplight in front of the old houses. A calmer alternative is Siddhidas Marg, a short walk away, where the shophouses give a quieter backdrop. Expect narrow lanes with vehicles and rickshaws, so keep an eye on your surroundings while you frame your shot.
text.geographic_location: Indra Chowk lies in the old city of Kathmandu, on the historic market street that links Kathmandu Durbar Square with Asan. The Akash Bhairav temple stands on the western side of the square.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or stops nearby, so head for the old town around Kathmandu Durbar Square and continue on foot. From the Durbar Square and Makhan side, the street leads to the south-western corner of Indra Chowk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the temple and the junction together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane is too tight to fit the shrine and the houses around it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the shrine window and lamps without walking into worshippers' space.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Akash Bhairav Temple (west side of the square, upper floor reached by external staircase). The temple's upper-floor window and the lamp-lit shrine area, framed against the old merchant houses around the junction. From here your photo shows the temple's upper-floor window and the lamp-lit shrine area, framed against the old merchant houses around the junction.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the shrine window on one third of the frame, with the old house fronts filling the rest. Wait for a gap in the people and rickshaws before you press the shutter. If the square is too crowded, try Siddhidas Marg, a calmer street of shophouses nearby, for a quieter shot of old Kathmandu architecture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the shrine or the brightest lamp to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the flames keep their glow. At dusk, let night mode work and hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep it still. Try a Live Photo to catch movement in the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk is best, especially during Indra Jatra in September, when the oil lamps are lit. Expect the square to be very crowded and the street layout to change during the festival.

text.access_note: The square and the temple are in public space and can be seen without a ticket; check local signs before you go, as photography rules and access to the upper floor may vary.

name: Kathmandu Durbar Square
label: Kathmandu Durbar Sq.
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shiva-Parvati Temple' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Shiva Parvati Temple' (way/185882281): middle (24 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/247501389: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gaddi Baithak' (66 m across).
notes: Historic royal palace square with temples and courtyards.

text.description:
Kathmandu Durbar Square, also known as Hanuman Dhoka or Basantapur Durbar Kshetra, is the old royal square of the city. It is one of three Durbar Squares in the Kathmandu Valley that are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The outer part has a number of 16th-century temples from the Malla kings, with finely carved Newar facades. The palace buildings around the central space date from the Malla and Shah periods. The best known is the nine-storey Nautalle Durbar, built by Prithvi Narayan Shah to mark the Unification of Nepal. The Kumari Ghar, home of the Kumari, stands at the southern edge. The earthquake of 25 April 2015 badly damaged the square, and the old wooden Kasthamandap was among the buildings lost.

It photographs well because so much is packed into one view: carved wooden windows, tiered temple roofs, palace brickwork and the daily life of the square in front. A good place to start is the Shiva-Parvati Temple on the western side. Its painted wooden figures of Shiva and Parvati lean out of an upper window, and the busy square sits below them. Guides describe it as one of the most photographed spots in Kathmandu. Take a few frames with people in them for scale, then a few without if you can wait for a gap. Some areas have rules about photography, so look for signs and follow them, especially around the Kumari Ghar.
text.geographic_location: Kathmandu Durbar Square is in Kathmandu, Nepal. The Shiva-Parvati Temple is on the western side of the square.
text.directions_text: No station or stop data is available for this spot, so use local directions to Kathmandu Durbar Square (Hanuman Dhoka). Once inside, head for the western side of the square to find the Shiva-Parvati Temple. The main part of the square and the palace buildings lie to the south-east, and the Kumari Ghar is at the southern edge of the square. The ticket counter is by the Hanuman statue, so check the official site before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the temple, the window figures and the square around them. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the painted figures and the carved wood. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the whole square, and keep people and the temple away from the edges, where it stretches shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Shiva-Parvati Temple (western side of the square, first-floor window). The painted wooden figures of Shiva and Parvati leaning from the upper window, with the busy square in the foreground. On the western side of the square. From here you see the painted wooden figures of Shiva and Parvati leaning from the first-floor window, with the busy square in front. The palace buildings and the main part of the square are to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the window on one of the upper lines, leaving the square and its people in the lower part of the frame. For a wider view, Kumari Ghar shows its carved wooden balconies and courtyard-facing front from the square. Cafe Soma gives a raised view over the temple roofs and palace buildings, and it is a café, so you would normally buy something there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the painted figures to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky or white walls make the window look dark. Take a few shots in a row, because people will keep moving through the frame. Do not photograph the Kumari herself, and do not take photos inside the Kumari Bahal courtyard or the palace museums.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early, before about 7:30 AM. One guide says the square is quieter then and the morning light is better.

text.access_note: This is a historic square with a monument zone that foreign visitors may need a ticket to enter, and photography is banned in some areas, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The palace buildings and the main part of the square lie to the south-east of the Shiva-Parvati Temple.
Using the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) near the edges of the frame can stretch shapes.
Bright sky or white walls can make a shaded window look dark on a phone, and lowering the exposure slider can help.
People will keep moving through the frame, so a few shots in a row help.

name: Boudhanath
label: Boudhanath Stupa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Best View Restaurant' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Best View Restaurant' (node/4555227689): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q889902: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: One of the largest spherical stupas in the world.

text.description:
Boudhanath is the great white stupa at the heart of Boudha, in the north-east of Kathmandu. It is the largest spherical stupa in Nepal and one of the largest in the world, and it has been a stopping place for Tibetan traders and pilgrims for centuries. The present structure was most likely built in the 14th century, though local chronicles mention a stupa here as early as the 5th century. It was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979. After 1959 many Tibetan refugees settled around it, and the square is now ringed by more than 50 monasteries, plus restaurants, guesthouses and craft shops.

It photographs well because the white dome, the painted eyes and the pilgrims moving around the base all sit together in one frame. For a calmer, higher view, try the rooftop terrace of Best View Restaurant, inside the Boudhanath complex. Visitors describe it as a good, quieter place to see the stupa, with a close view framed by the buildings around the square. If you want a second angle, the rooftop above Guru Lhakhang monastery shows the dome and eyes with the pilgrims' circuit below, and the stupa is floodlit there at night. Keep your phone ready for the pilgrims, but ask before photographing monks or people at prayer.
text.geographic_location: Boudhanath stands in the Boudha area in the north-east of Kathmandu, on the edge of the Kathmandu Valley. It is surrounded by Tibetan monasteries, guesthouses and cafés.
text.directions_text: Boudha lies in the north-east of Kathmandu, so head there from the centre of the city and ask for the Boudhanath stupa. The Best View Restaurant rooftop terrace is inside the Boudhanath complex; confirm its name and location on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the framed view from the rooftop. Switch to the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the painted eyes and the pilgrims below. Try ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole dome with the rooftops around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Best View Restaurant (rooftop terrace, Boudhanath complex). A close, framed view of the stupa from a rooftop terrace inside the Boudhanath complex. For a higher view, use the rooftop terrace of Best View Restaurant, inside the Boudhanath complex, once you have confirmed its name and location on the map. From there you get a close view of the stupa framed by the square around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on one side with the spire reaching upwards. Let the rooftop edge or the prayer flags make a frame. If you can, include a few pilgrims at the base for scale. For a different angle, try the rooftop above Guru Lhakhang, or look down on the pilgrims from the stupa's own raised level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white dome to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white does not turn grey or lose its detail. Live Photos can catch the pilgrims moving around the base. Use night mode if you are there when the stupa is floodlit, and brace your elbows on the rail to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white dome. After dark the floodlit stupa is worth a night-mode photo.

text.access_note: Boudhanath is a place of worship with its own rules. The stupa charges an entrance fee, and access to restaurant or monastery rooftops may require a purchase or fee. Follow any posted rules on flash, and ask permission before photographing monks.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light on the white dome.
From a close rooftop the whole dome may only fit in the ultra-wide (0.5x) view.

name: Dharahara
label: Dharahara Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dharahara' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5269090: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Rebuilt landmark tower in central Kathmandu.

text.description:
Dharahara is a tall, slim white tower in the centre of Sundhara, built in the early 1830s as a watchtower and rebuilt after the 2015 earthquake brought most of it down. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, so you can take two kinds of photo from one spot. From the ground, the tower rises against the sky with street and park life around its foot. From the glass observation deck, you get a wide view over the Kathmandu Valley: rooftops, temples and, on clear days, the distant hills and Himalayas.

Some facts help you plan. The tower is about 72 metres tall and keeps its traditional minaret shape with a bronze mast on top. The rebuilt tower was inaugurated in April 2021 and opened fully to the public in September 2024. A museum, a garden and a fountain sit close by. The remains of the original base are still there, and a close-up of the broken brickwork beside the new tower makes a good contrast with the wide views.

The exact floor count and deck details may vary, so check these on the day. For the best photos, take one wide shot from the ground to show the whole tower. Then go up and shoot the valley in overlapping sections for a stitched panorama.
text.geographic_location: Dharahara stands at the centre of Sundhara in central Kathmandu. The old military parade ground, Tundikhel, lies to its north-east.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot, so head for Sundhara in central Kathmandu and look for the tower. The tower is tall enough to see from the surrounding streets, so you can walk the last stretch towards it. Tundikhel is to the north-east of the tower, which helps you check your bearings. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the foot of the tower to fit the whole height in from close range. On the deck, use the default lens (1x) for the main valley view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out distant hills and temple roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the valley panorama, go up to the glass observation deck and use the east side for the city view. From there you see rooftops, temples and, on clear days, the distant hills and Himalayas. As an alternative, shoot the white tower against the sky from the ground, with the street and park life below it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: On the deck, use panorama mode, or take several overlapping shots to stitch together, sweeping slowly from left to right. If the glass is dusty, use any open sections to shoot through. On the ground, turn on gridlines to keep the tower upright, and tilt the phone up as little as you can. For a different shot, move in close on the broken original base next to the rebuilt tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the distant hills to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady against your body, and wipe the lens before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is best for mountain views. Late afternoon gives better light on the city.

text.access_note: The tower grounds can be seen from outside, but the observation deck needs an entry ticket, so check the official site before you go for current details.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting the phone upwards from close range makes vertical lines lean inwards, so stepping back or using the ultra-wide lens helps.
Dragging the exposure slider down helps keep detail in a bright sky.
Wiping the phone lens before shooting improves sharpness and reduces glare.

name: Narayanhiti Palace Museum
label: Narayanhiti Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Durbar Marg' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Traffic Police Durbar Marg' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1050042: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: Narayanhiti Palace Museum is the former royal palace of Nepal, opened to the public as a museum in 2008 after the monarchy ended. The palace you see today was ordered by King Mahendra in 1963 and finished in 1969. It was designed by the American architect Benjamin Polk, who used Nepalese building styles so that it would read as a national symbol. It photographs well because it fronts straight onto the road. From Durbar Marg, the wide front facade and entrance gate line up down the length of the avenue, which gives a clean, balanced frontal shot. A tall central tower rises above the front, built over a Hindu temple, and it makes a good detail to pick out with zoom. The name comes from Narayana, a form of Vishnu whose temple stands opposite, and from a traditional stone water spout east of the main entrance. Photography is not allowed inside the palace buildings, and phones are left at the gate cloakroom, so this spot is about the outside view. The street is busy with shops and cafes, so expect people and vehicles in the frame. If you want a quieter angle, Narayanhiti Path runs along the walled compound and gives glimpses of the grounds over the wall.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in central Kathmandu, east of the Kaiser Mahal and next to the Thamel area. It sits on Durbar Marg, with the Narayana (Vishnu) temple opposite.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Thamel, the well-known area next to the palace. Durbar Marg is easy to reach on foot from there. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Durbar Marg or the Narayanhiti Palace Museum. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the facade and gate. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the avenue and the full width of the palace will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the central tower and the gate details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Durbar Marg (opposite the main palace gate, at the north end of the avenue). The palace's grand front facade and entrance gate framed down the length of the avenue, with the palace fronting directly on the road. For the frontal shot, walk up Durbar Marg to the spot opposite the main palace gate. From that position the front facade and entrance gate are framed down the length of the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the gate up with the centre of the frame so the symmetry works. Keep the phone level so the facade does not lean, and let the road lead the eye towards the palace. For a quieter alternative, walk along Narayanhiti Path and shoot along the compound wall, using the wall as a leading line.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. Wait for a gap in the traffic and people before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight when the sun is not directly overhead, such as morning or late afternoon, should give softer, more even light on the facade. Earlier in the day the street is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The museum itself is a ticketed site with no photography inside the palace buildings, and opening days may vary, so check the official site before you go; the view from the street is free.

name: Kasthamandap
label: Kasthamandap
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Basantapur Durbar Square' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Durbar Square Ticket Counter' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/183558418: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kasthamandap' (36 m across).
notes: Ancient pavilion rebuilt after the 2015 earthquake.

text.description:
Kasthamandap is a three-tiered wooden pavilion in Kathmandu Durbar Square. Its name means "wood-covered shelter", and it served as a public shelter as well as a temple. The original was destroyed in the April 2015 earthquake, and the building you see now is a reconstruction. Digs after the quake found that the oldest parts date to the 7th century CE. A shrine to the saint Gorakshanath was added inside much later.

The pavilion photographs best as part of the square around it. From here you get the pagoda-style roofline in the distance, with pigeons, street vendors and everyday city life in the foreground. That mix makes a livelier picture than a plain record shot of the building.

The pavilion will look fairly small from here, so use the telephoto lens to bring it closer. A second option is to walk to the pavilion itself for its carved struts and layered roof. Photography inside the pavilion is prohibited. Scaffolding may still be in place, depending on the stage of the reconstruction work, so look at the current state of the building before you plan your shot.
text.geographic_location: Kasthamandap stands in Kathmandu Durbar Square, in the old city of Kathmandu, among the temples and palace buildings of the historic square.
text.directions_text: No stations are listed nearby, so navigate to Basantapur Durbar Square on foot or by whatever local transport you prefer. The pavilion lies to the west of it, about 340 m on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the pavilion closer across the square. Use the default lens (1x) when you want the pigeons, vendors and square all in one picture. The ultra-wide (0.5x) works for the foreground only if you keep the pavilion away from the edges, where buildings can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Basantapur Durbar Square (open ground in front of the pavilion, looking across the square). The pavilion within the busy square, with pigeons, street vendors and everyday life in the foreground. On the open ground in front of the pavilion, and look west across the square. A closer alternative is to walk up to the pavilion itself for its main facade, with carved struts and pagoda roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put a few pigeons or a passing vendor in the lower third of the frame and the pavilion in the upper part, so the picture shows the building in its everyday setting. Turn on gridlines and keep the roof lines level. For a tighter shot of the pavilion, zoom in rather than walk into the crowd. Another option is a raised view over the whole square from Taleju Temple, but check on site whether that works for this building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo to catch pigeons taking off, and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer in the square, with fewer people crossing your frame.

text.access_note: The square is part of a paid complex, and the pavilion's ticket is included in the Durbar Square ticket for foreigners, so check the official site before you go; photography inside the pavilion is prohibited.

name: Rani Pokhari
label: Rani Pokhari
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rani Pokhari' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/21565774: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rani Pokhari' (213 m across).
notes: Historic pond with a small temple at its centre.

text.description:
Rani Pokhari is a large, square, man-made pond in the middle of Kathmandu, and it works well as a calm photo stop in a busy part of the city. A temple stands on an island at the centre, and on still water its white shape is mirrored in the pond, with trees and greenery around the edge. That reflection is the picture most visitors come for.

King Pratap Malla had the pond built in 1670 for his queen, who was grieving after their son was killed by an elephant. It measures about 180 m by 140 m. The temple was rebuilt after the 2015 earthquake and the work was finished in October 2020. It is now in the older Shikhara style rather than the dome style many people remember. Nearby you can also pick out the Ghanta Ghar clock tower across the road to the east, and a stone elephant statue on the southern bank.

For your phone, shoot from the pond's edge on the entrance side, and keep the temple and its reflection centred. Wait for a moment when the surface is still, as ripples break the mirror effect. Sunrise or sunset gives the strongest reflection. The temple is white, so check your screen for blown-out highlights and darken the exposure a touch if needed. If you want a different angle, one traveller review mentions the Jamal Overhead Bridge as a higher viewpoint, but check that it is accessible.
text.geographic_location: Rani Pokhari lies in central Kathmandu, on the eastern edge of the old city, just outside a former city gate. The Ghanta Ghar clock tower and Tri Chandra College are across the road to the east, and the Jamal area is on its north-western corner.
text.directions_text: Head for the Ghanta Ghar clock tower in central Kathmandu, which stands across the road from the pond's eastern side. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for Rani Pokhari or Ghanta Ghar. The entrance side of the pond is where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the temple with its reflection. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole pond, the trees and the sky in one frame. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it to pick out the temple's roof and details across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the white temple, its reflection in the still water and the greenery around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the temple on the centre line so it and its reflection balance top and bottom. Keep the phone level so the water's edge stays straight. Include a little of the surrounding trees to frame it. For a higher view, one traveller review mentions the Jamal Overhead Bridge as a viewpoint, but check that it is accessible before relying on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the temple to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the white walls keep their detail. Take a Live Photo or a short burst and pick the frame where the water is calmest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when the reflection is strongest.

text.access_note: The pond is fenced and the temple is open to the public only on certain festival days, so photograph from outside and check the official site or local information for current access before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ripples on the water reduce the mirror effect of the reflection.
A white building can lose detail in bright light, so lowering the exposure slightly helps.
Not every phone has a telephoto lens, and the zoom range varies between models.
Drones are generally restricted in this historic area, so assume they are not allowed.

name: Singha Durbar
label: Singha Durbar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Singha Durbar Marg' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Traffic Police Durbar Marg' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/13277054059: the OpenStreetMap point 'Singha Durbar'.
notes: Grand Rana-era palace, now government offices.

text.description:
Singha Durbar, the 'Lion's Palace', is a large palace complex in the middle of Kathmandu. Chandra Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana built it in 1908. It began as a small private home but grew during construction, and was soon sold to the Government of Nepal as the Prime Minister's residence. Its design blends Palladian, Neoclassical and Baroque styles, which is why the white façade looks so grand. Today it houses government offices, including the Federal Parliament. It has been through a lot: a major fire in 1973, when the front-facing wing was spared, serious damage in the 2015 earthquake, and another fire during the protests of September 2025. What you see now may differ from older pictures.

The gate-and-façade photo is taken from Singha Durbar Marg, the road opposite the main gate with the lion statues. From there the gate and the palace front are easy to fit into one frame. Stay outside the walls: photography inside the complex, and of government activity, is prohibited. Keep your shots to the gate, the lions and the façade, and avoid pointing the phone at guards or officials. Because the site was damaged in 2025, check locally or on an official site before you go, in case access around the complex has changed.
text.geographic_location: Singha Durbar sits in central Kathmandu, east of Bhadrakali Temple and north of Babar Mahal and Thapathali Durbar. The area around it is now called Bhadrakali Plaza.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground-style stations or tram stops to use here, so go by taxi or hired scooter from the nearest well-known area, such as Babar Mahal, Thapathali or Bhadrakali Temple. For the gate-and-façade shot, ask to be dropped on Singha Durbar Marg, the road in front of the main gate with the lion statues, which is about 1.9 km south of the marker. The complex lies just east of Bhadrakali Temple, so you can use the temple as a landmark. Check locally that the road is open before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the gate, so the gate and the full palace front fit in. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the lion statues and the façade details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Singha Durbar Marg (opposite the main gate with the lion statues). The lion-marked main gate and the grand white façade of the palace, framed from the road in front of the complex. For the gate-and-façade shot, walk or ride to Singha Durbar Marg, opposite the main gate with the lion statues. From there your photo shows the lion-marked main gate and the white front of the palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the gate on the central vertical line so the building looks balanced. Keep the phone level, so the tall façade doesn't lean. For a second picture, zoom in on a lion statue with the palace blurred behind it. A raised view over the rooftops from Dharahara has also been suggested, but treat it as unconfirmed and check it is open first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white doesn't turn flat and bright. Turn on gridlines to keep the lines straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning and late afternoon, according to a visitor guide.

text.access_note: Singha Durbar Marg is a street, but check locally that access is open. Photography inside the complex and of government activity is prohibited, and access may have changed since the 2025 damage, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Sliding the exposure down on a bright white façade helps keep detail, which is general phone-camera practice.
Guards or officials may ask visitors to move on or stop photographing near a government complex.
Nearby roads may carry traffic, so stand on the pavement rather than in the road.

name: Asan
label: Asan Bazaar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Asan Tol' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/31019262: the OpenStreetMap point 'Asan Tol'.
notes: Lively old market crossroads with temples.

text.description: Asan is the busiest crossing in Kathmandu's old city, a market square where six streets meet. Vendors sell spices, vegetables, textiles and much more, and small shrines sit around the edges, so one frame can hold a lot of daily life. Its Annapurna Ajimā temple, dedicated to the goddess of abundant grain, presides over the square. There is also a Ganesh temple on the northern side, with tile roofs replaced in 1928, and a small Narayan shrine on the northwestern side. At the centre stands the stone fish called Nyālon, tied to the legend of how Asan was founded. The square sits on one of the two legendary India-Tibet trade routes through Kathmandu, which is why it has been a main marketplace since ancient times. It photographs best as a wide, busy scene: stalls in the foreground, shrines and lanes behind, and people moving through. Go early if you can, because the light is softer and the square is quieter. Keep your phone ready for quick shots, but ask vendors and passers-by before taking close-up portraits. If you want a calmer picture, move in on one detail, such as a pile of spices, the fish stone or a shrine roof, rather than trying to fit everything in.
text.geographic_location: Asan is in the old city of central Kathmandu, a market and ceremonial square where six streets meet. It lies along the old trade route that runs from Kathmandu Durbar Square.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so head for the old city of central Kathmandu and ask for Asan, also spelt Asan Tole. You can come by taxi or bus; two taxi stands and bus stops are on the eastern side of the square. Once there, walk to the middle of the square, between the potted trees by the small Narayan shrine, which is where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole junction, the stalls and the shrines into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of people and vendors. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the Annapurna temple roofs, spices or flower sellers without walking into the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Asan Tol, near the centre of the square, between the potted trees by the small Narayan shrine. From here you get a wide view of the crowded junction where the market lanes meet, with the vegetable and spice vendors and the Ganesh and Narayan shrines around the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon and building edges straight, then let the market lanes lead the eye into the picture. Include a vendor or a shrine in the foreground for a sense of scale. For a second, closer picture, the Annapurna Temple is a good alternative: its three-roofed pagoda-style shrine framed by market stalls, flower sellers and passing locals.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the shrine roofs and sky keep their detail. In a crowd, try a Live Photo to catch the best moment of movement. Ask before taking close-up portraits.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is softer and the square is less crowded.

text.access_note: Asan is an open public market square, but the shrines and courtyards around it are places of worship, so be respectful and check locally before you go.

name: Maitighar Mandala
label: Maitighar Mandala
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Maitighar Mandala' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/120106732: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Maitighar Mandala' (35 m across).

text.description: Maitighar Mandala is a large painted circle set into a traffic island in the middle of Kathmandu. Seen from above it is a pattern of concentric rings, but at street level you read it as a bold, colourful disc with greenery around it and the national flag at the centre. That makes it an easy, graphic subject for a phone. The outer ring has 32 vajras, the next has 16 lotus petals, and the innermost ring has 32 garlands. The colours stand for human qualities: black for anger, orange for love and blue for compassion. At the four corners are symbols of the Ashtamangal. The mandala was built in 2001 for the 11th SAARC summit and later restored. The traffic island is busy, and the mandala sits recessed, so it is hard to see from the road itself. The pedestrian walkway around the island is the better place to look at it. Take your time on the footpath and keep well back from the kerb. Shoot the whole pattern first, then move in for details such as the vajras or petals. The area is a busy junction, so expect noise and vehicles in the background. Wear your wrist strap if you have one, and keep your phone away from the road edge when you are framing a shot. Gatherings are frequent here and can change access, so be flexible.
text.geographic_location: Maitighar Mandala is in the centre of Kathmandu, on an island where the roads from Thapathali, New Baneshwor and Bhadrakali meet. It lies at the south-east corner of Singha Durbar, the administrative centre of Nepal.
text.directions_text: Start from the Thapathali, New Baneshwor or Singha Durbar area of central Kathmandu and head for the road junction where the three roads meet. From further away, head for the Maitighar junction in central Kathmandu. Once there, use the pedestrian walkway around the traffic island rather than crossing the carriageways. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full circle and the greenery around it. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the vajras, lotus petals and the flag at the centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your shot from the pedestrian walkway at the edge of the island, as close to the subject as is safe, and never stand in the carriageway. From the walkway you can see the concentric rings, vajras and lotus-petal motifs, with the national flag at the centre and greenery around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the flag at the centre of the frame so the rings look balanced. Hold the phone level, since a tilt makes the circles look lopsided. Then move closer or zoom in for a detail shot of the petals or vajras. Keep to the pedestrian edge and watch the traffic while you compose.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the screen to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the colours stay rich and the sky is not washed out. After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone as still as you can, resting your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening or night, when the coloured lights are on. Daytime also works for clear colours.

text.access_note: This is an open public traffic island with a pedestrian walkway, but protests and gatherings are frequent and can block or change access, so check the situation on the day.

name: Kumari Ghar
label: Kumari Ghar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kumari Ghar' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N2659104413 (Kumari Ghar): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Carved wooden palace of the living goddess.

text.description:
Kumari Ghar is a three-storey red-brick building on the southern side of Basantapur Durbar Square. Its carved wooden windows and balconies are the main reason to photograph it, and they show off Newar architecture well. The brickwork gives you a warm, solid background, and the dark timber carving stands out against it.

The best shot is the front of the building from the square outside the entrance, near the two white lion statues. The lions make a useful foreground, and the carved facade rises behind them. A second option is the gateway area. The entrance area is also called Kumari Chowk. Use the same idea there: lions low in the frame, windows above.

The building is a religious residence, so treat it with care. Never photograph the Kumari herself. Guides advise putting your phone away if she appears at a window. Check on the day whether you can photograph the inner courtyard, and look for signs on site and follow them. Stay in public areas and do not block any ceremonial route while you line up your shot.

Give yourself a few minutes for the carved details. Walk a little to either side of the entrance to find a clean angle without too many people in it. Take one wide shot of the whole facade, then move closer for the windows.
text.geographic_location: Kumari Ghar is in the southern part of Basantapur Durbar Square, in the old centre of Kathmandu. It stands near the two white lion statues at the entrance.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport stop at this spot, so head for Basantapur Durbar Square in the old part of Kathmandu. Walk to the southern part of the square, where you will see the two white lion statues at the entrance. The phone icon on the map is right in front of the building, so you will not need to walk further. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded or you cannot step back far enough to fit all three storeys. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved windows and balconies.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the building. From here the photo shows the three-storey red-brick facade with its carved wooden windows and balconies, framed from the square outside the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the facade does not lean. Put one or both lion statues low in the foreground and let the carved windows fill the upper frame. For a different view, try the gateway area (also called Kumari Chowk), with the lions in front and the carved facade behind. Photograph the building only, never the Kumari.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the carved woodwork to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the red brick keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. Skip portrait mode here, as it can blur the carving you want sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when sunlight lights the carved woodwork, according to one guide.

text.access_note: Entry to Durbar Square is ticketed for foreigners, and the building is a religious residence, so check the official site before you go and follow any signs about photography.

name: Kaal Bhairav
label: Kaal Bhairav
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Basantapur Durbar Square' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Durbar Square Ticket Counter' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/196261745: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kal Bhairab Temple' (10 m across).
notes: Large stone statue of the fierce deity at Durbar Square.

text.description:
Kaal Bhairav is a Hindu shrine in Kathmandu Durbar Square, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The statue is a fierce, dark figure with six arms. It stands over a trampled figure, Betal, and sits in front of the Hanuman Dhoka palace. That combination of dark carved stone and old palace walls gives you a strong, layered picture even on a phone.

According to legend, the figure was found in a paddy field and later moved to the Durbar Square by King Pratap Malla. It is believed to have been carved from a single stone. These are good facts to remember when you are deciding what to include in the frame.

Walk about 300 m west to reach the statue, on the northwest side of the square in front of the Hanuman Dhoka palace. There you can show the statue together with the palace behind it, so the picture says where you are as well as what you are looking at. Take one wide shot for the setting, then move closer for the details: the raised arms, the face and the figure underneath.

This is a working place of worship. Devotees often pray at the statue, so a clear frontal shot may take a little patience. Wait for a gap rather than asking people to move. If you want a very close, head-on view of the statue itself, the area right in front of it gives that, with offerings and lamps often placed at the base.
text.geographic_location: Kaal Bhairav is in Kathmandu Durbar Square, in the old centre of Kathmandu. It stands in front of the Hanuman Dhoka palace.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Kathmandu Durbar Square in the old town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the statue with the palace behind it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the face, arms and the figure underneath without pushing through the crowd. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close, and keep the statue away from the edges, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Basantapur Durbar Square (northwest side of the square, where the statue stands in front of the Hanuman Dhoka palace). The black stone Kaal Bhairav statue, with its six arms and the trampled Betal below, standing before the Hanuman Dhoka palace. Once you are there, you can see the black stone statue with its six arms and the trampled Betal below, with the palace behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the statue on one of the vertical lines, with the palace wall filling the space behind. Take one wide shot, then a tighter telephoto shot of the arms and face. For a close, frontal view of the statue, with offerings and lamps often at its base, go and stand in front of it. Keep a clear path for people who have come to pray.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the dark stone keeps its detail and the bright sky or palace does not wash out. Live Photos can catch the moment if someone offers a flower or lights a lamp, but ask permission before photographing devotees close up.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Devotees often pray at the statue, so a clear frontal shot may need patience.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship in Kathmandu Durbar Square, so dress respectfully, and check the official site before you go for any entry rules for the square.

name: Taleju Temple
label: Taleju Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hanuman Dhoka' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hanuman Dhoka' (node/11365076769): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1414600808: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Taleju Temple' (78 m across).
notes: Tall multi-roofed temple beside the old palace.

text.description: Taleju Temple is a Hindu temple dedicated to Taleju Bhawani, the royal patron goddess of the Malla dynasty. Mahendra Malla built it in 1564, and it stands in Hanuman Dhoka, part of Kathmandu Durbar Square, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is a tall, pagoda-style building, so its stacked roofs and upper plinth are the main things to photograph. The temple opens only once a year, at Dashain, so every photo here is of the outside. The usual picture is taken from the busy courtyard floor. For a calmer angle, climb the short flight of steps at Hanuman Dhoka, on the side opposite the courtyard, and turn back towards the temple. That gives you a slightly raised view with fewer people in front of you. Light and composition change the result a lot, so take a few frames and compare them. If you want the full height of the temple rising above the square, Basantapur Square is a good second position. Keep your phone steady against your body, and watch for people passing on the steps.
text.geographic_location: Taleju Temple is in Hanuman Dhoka, within Kathmandu Durbar Square, in the historic centre of Kathmandu. Confirm the exact steps on site.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed nearby, so just head for Kathmandu Durbar Square. Once inside the square area, look for the steps at Hanuman Dhoka on the side opposite the courtyard. Confirm the exact position of the steps on the ground. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the temple together with some of the square. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the roof tiers and carved details without walking closer. Ultra-wide (0.5x) suits the steps and courtyard, but it makes the temple look small and far away.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hanuman Dhoka (steps on the side opposite the Durbar Square courtyard, turning back toward the temple). A quieter, elevated angle on the temple, shot from a short climb of steps rather than from the crowded courtyard floor. On the side opposite the Durbar Square courtyard, and turn back towards the temple, which lies to the north-east. From here you get a quieter, slightly raised angle, rather than the usual view from the crowded courtyard floor.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the temple's upright lines parallel to the edges of the screen. Let the roofs fill the upper part of the frame and use the steps or courtyard as a foreground. For a different view showing the full height of the temple above the square, try Basantapur Square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the roofs do not wash out. Take a Live Photo too, in case people walk through the frame at the wrong moment and you want to pick a better one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Close to sunset or on a sunny morning.

text.access_note: Kathmandu Durbar Square is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where visitors may need a ticket, and the temple itself opens only at Dashain and has been reported as under renovation, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ghanta Ghar
label: Ghanta Ghar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rani Pokhari' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rani Pokhari' (way/21565774): middle (213 m across); moved 40 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/194744621: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Trichandra Campus' (17 m across).
notes: Clock tower at Tri-Chandra campus near Ratna Park.

text.description:
Ghanta Ghar is the oldest clock tower in Nepal, and its name simply means "Hour House". It was built under the Rana prime minister Bir Shumsher and was modelled on Big Ben in London, a sign of the Western influence that reached Nepali architecture in the Rana era. The tower you see today was rebuilt on the original site after the earthquake of 1990 BS (1934) brought the first one down.

It photographs well because it is tall and plain against the sky. The pond at Rani Pokhari offers a separate option: a calm stretch of water to put in front of the tower, with the temple and the surrounding trees framing it on either side. That makes a tidy, layered picture even on a crowded day.

Keep the phone straight and use the gridlines so the tower does not lean. The default lens (1x) gives a natural view of the whole scene. If you want the tower to fill more of the frame, step up to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone). If you are close to the tower or tight against the water's edge, the ultra-wide (0.5x) will fit in the whole tower, but it will make the tower look smaller and may bend its edges. Wait for people and vehicles to clear before you tap. Tundikhel, the open parade ground nearby, is a good second spot, with the tower as a backdrop to the wide space.
text.geographic_location: Ghanta Ghar stands in central Kathmandu, in front of the Rani Pokhari pond and close to Trichandra College. It is described as being on Durbar Marg and also near Ratnapark, so it is easiest to find by name on the map.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground or tram stop for this spot, so head for central Kathmandu and look for the pond at Rani Pokhari. Because it is described as being on Durbar Marg and also near Ratnapark, the easiest way is to search for "Ghanta Ghar" on the map and head for the tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower and its surroundings together. Use the telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the tower, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the pond and the temple.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rani Pokhari (pond's western edge, shooting east across the water toward the tower). The clock tower rising behind the still water of the pond, with the temple and surrounding trees framing the tower. For a view across the pond at Rani Pokhari, with the temple and trees on either side, adjust your position until the tower sits clearly behind the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight. If you are using the pond view, put the water in the lower part of the frame and the tower in the upper half, and let the temple and trees fill the sides. For a different view, try Tundikhel, where the tower stands behind the open parade ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. If the water is calm, hold the phone steady for a sharper reflection. Live Photos can help you catch a moment when people or traffic clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. In April and May the jacaranda blossom around Tundikhel and Ghanta Ghar adds colour.

text.access_note: The tower and pond sit in a busy public area of the city. Check locally for closures or photography restrictions at Rani Pokhari before you go.
